title: How a Refrigerator Works, and How to Use Yours Well
summary: A fridge doesn't make cold; it moves heat. Here is what the compressor, condenser, capillary tube and evaporator each do, plus the right temperatures, where to store food, and how to save energy.
body:
Open the refrigerator door and a small light comes on, a puff of cold air rolls out over your feet, and somewhere at the back a quiet hum starts or stops. It is probably the hardest-working machine in your home: it runs day and night, every day, for ten or fifteen years, and most of us only think about it when the milk goes sour.

Yet the fridge is a small marvel of physics. It does something that seems to break the ordinary rules of nature: it moves heat from a cold place (the inside of the box) to a warm place (your kitchen). Left alone, heat always flows the other way, from hot to cold. A fridge makes it run uphill, and it does so with a handful of parts and one clever fluid.

This guide explains how a refrigerator works, what each part does, why the back or sides feel warm, how a freezer stays frost-free, what the numbers on the label mean, and, most practically, how to set, load and look after your fridge so that food stays safe and the electricity bill stays low.

## The big idea: a fridge does not make cold, it moves heat

The first thing to understand is that "cold" is not a substance. There is no such thing as adding cold to a box. Cold is simply the absence of heat. To make the inside of the fridge cold, the machine has to pick up heat from the food and the air inside and carry it somewhere else.

That "somewhere else" is your kitchen. A refrigerator is, in effect, a heat pump: a device that pumps heat out of one space and dumps it into another. That is why the coils on the back or the panels on the sides of a modern fridge feel warm, and why a room with a fridge in it never gets colder overall. In fact the room gets very slightly warmer, because the heat dumped outside includes not only the heat taken from inside but also the energy used by the motor.

This also explains a classic myth. Leaving the refrigerator door open on a hot day will not cool the kitchen. The fridge will just run constantly, pulling heat from the front and releasing it, plus extra motor heat, out of the back, into the same room.

## The secret ingredient: evaporation absorbs heat

How do you pick up heat and carry it? Nature offers a simple trick, one you feel every time you step out of a swimming pool on a breezy day. As water evaporates from your skin, you feel cold. Turning a liquid into a gas takes energy, and the liquid takes that energy as heat from whatever it touches.

The reverse is also true. When a gas condenses back into a liquid, it releases that heat. Steam scalds partly because it dumps a lot of heat into your skin as it condenses.

A refrigerator uses a special fluid called a **refrigerant**, chosen because it boils at a very low temperature, well below the freezing point of water, at ordinary pressures. The trick is to control the pressure:

- At **low pressure**, the refrigerant boils at a very low temperature, so it can evaporate inside the cold fridge and soak up heat even there.
- At **high pressure**, the same refrigerant condenses at a temperature higher than your kitchen, so it can give up that heat to the room.

By squeezing the refrigerant and then letting it expand again, over and over, the fridge makes it evaporate where we want cold and condense where we don't mind heat. This loop is called the **vapor-compression cycle**, and it is the heart of almost every household refrigerator, air conditioner and heat pump in the world.

## The four main parts

A standard fridge has four key components connected in a sealed loop of copper or aluminium tubing. The refrigerant circulates through them endlessly.

### 1. The compressor: the heart

The compressor is the black, roughly football-sized metal canister you can see near the bottom at the back of most fridges. Inside is an electric motor driving a small pump. It sucks in cool, low-pressure refrigerant gas and squeezes it into a hot, high-pressure gas.

Compressing a gas heats it up, the same reason a bicycle pump gets warm when you inflate a tyre. After the compressor, the refrigerant may be considerably hotter than the room. That matters: heat only flows from hot to cold, so to shed heat into a warm kitchen, the refrigerant must first be hotter than the kitchen.

The hum you hear when the fridge "kicks in" is mostly the compressor running. When the inside reaches the set temperature, a thermostat or control board switches it off, and the fridge goes quiet.

### 2. The condenser: the radiator

From the compressor, the hot gas flows into the **condenser**, a long, winding tube designed to release heat. In older fridges this is the black grid of tubes and wires on the back. In many modern models, the condenser tubes are hidden under the outer metal skin of the sides, or sit underneath with a small fan blowing over them. This is why the sides of some fridges feel warm to the touch; that is normal.

As the hot refrigerant gas travels through the condenser and gives its heat to the room, it cools enough to condense into a liquid, still under high pressure. Releasing that latent heat of condensation is the whole point of this stage.

### 3. The expansion device: the gatekeeper

Next, the high-pressure liquid has to become low-pressure again. In household fridges, this is usually done by a **capillary tube**: a very long, very thin copper tube, sometimes coiled, with an inner diameter of only around a millimetre. Larger systems often use an expansion valve instead.

As the liquid is forced through this narrow passage, its pressure drops sharply. The sudden pressure drop makes part of the liquid flash into vapor, and that partial boiling chills the whole mixture dramatically, down to temperatures well below freezing.

### 4. The evaporator: where the cold happens

The cold, low-pressure mixture now enters the **evaporator**, a set of tubes or a finned coil inside or just behind the freezer compartment. Here the refrigerant finally does its job. It is colder than anything in the fridge, so heat flows from the air and food into it. As it absorbs that heat, the remaining liquid boils into a gas.

In many fridges, a small fan circulates air over the evaporator and through ducts to the freezer and fresh-food compartments. The now-warmer, low-pressure gas then returns to the compressor, and the cycle starts again.

Put together, the loop looks like this:

1. Compressor squeezes cool gas into hot, high-pressure gas.
2. Condenser lets that gas release heat to the room and turn into a liquid.
3. Capillary tube or expansion valve drops the pressure, making the liquid very cold.
4. Evaporator lets the cold refrigerant absorb heat from inside the fridge and turn back into gas.

### The supporting cast

Around this core are several smaller parts that make a fridge practical:

- **Thermostat or electronic controller**: measures the temperature and switches the compressor on or off. The dial inside your fridge, often marked 1 to 5 or "colder/warmer", sets this. On many simple fridges, a higher number means colder, but check your manual, because some models do it the other way round.
- **Insulation**: the walls and door are filled with polyurethane foam. Good insulation is the biggest reason a modern fridge uses less energy than one from a few decades ago.
- **Door gasket**: the soft rubber or plastic seal around the door. It contains a magnetic strip that pulls the door shut and keeps warm air out.
- **Fans**: an evaporator fan moves cold air around the inside; in many models a condenser fan cools the condenser and compressor.
- **Defrost system**: on frost-free models, a heater, a timer or control board and a drain (more on this below).
- **Filter-drier**: a small canister in the refrigerant line that traps moisture and debris, which could otherwise freeze or block the capillary tube.

## Why your freezer is frost-free (and your old one was not)

Every time you open the door, warm, humid air rushes in. When that moist air touches the very cold evaporator, its water vapor freezes on the surface as frost, just as dew forms on cold grass at dawn. Over weeks, the frost builds up into thick ice.

Ice is a surprisingly good insulator. A thick layer on the evaporator blocks heat from reaching the refrigerant, so the fridge has to run longer and harder to keep cool. In older or simpler freezers, the owner had to switch the appliance off now and then, empty it, and let the ice melt. Many small fridges and chest freezers still work this way.

A **frost-free** (or "no frost") fridge automates this. The evaporator is hidden behind a panel, and the fan blows cold air past it into the compartments, which also keeps the food areas drier. At intervals, the control system stops the compressor and switches on a **defrost heater** attached to the evaporator coil for a short time. According to GE Appliances, older designs trigger defrost on a timer based on compressor run time (for example, every 8 to 15 hours of running), while "adaptive" systems decide when to defrost, often around once or twice a day. The frost melts, the water runs down a drain tube to a shallow pan at the bottom of the fridge, and there it evaporates back into the room. In many designs, the pan sits where warmth from the compressor or condenser helps the water evaporate.

This is why you may sometimes hear dripping or sizzling sounds from a frost-free fridge. It is the defrost cycle doing its job.

## The refrigerant story: from deadly to ozone-safe to climate-friendly

The history of refrigerants is a history of trading one problem for another.

The idea of mechanical refrigeration is old. The American inventor Jacob Perkins received a British patent in 1834 for an ice-making machine that used the vapor-compression principle, the same cycle described above. In the 1870s the German engineer Carl von Linde built improved compression machines, first using methyl ether (1874) and then ammonia (1876), which transformed brewing and industrial cooling.

Early home refrigerators of the 1910s and 1920s often used gases such as ammonia, methyl chloride or sulphur dioxide. They worked, but they were toxic or flammable, and leaks could be dangerous. In 1927, General Electric launched its "Monitor Top", a refrigerator with the compressor mounted on top in a round housing, which became one of the first widely sold, relatively affordable models.

Inventors also explored machines with no moving parts. In 1922 two Swedish students, Baltzar von Platen and Carl Munters, invented an **absorption refrigerator** that ran on heat instead of a motor-driven compressor; the rights were later acquired by Electrolux. Even Albert Einstein got involved: together with his former student Leo Szilard, he designed an absorption refrigerator with no moving parts, and they received a US patent for it in 1930. Absorption fridges are still used today in some camper vans, hotel minibars and off-grid homes because they can run on gas or other heat sources and are almost silent.

The breakthrough for safety came around 1928 to 1930, when Thomas Midgley Jr. and his colleagues, working for General Motors' Frigidaire division, developed dichlorodifluoromethane, a chlorofluorocarbon (CFC) better known as R-12 or by the trade name Freon. It was non-toxic and non-flammable, and it quickly became the standard refrigerant.

Decades later, scientists discovered that CFCs released into the air drift up to the stratosphere and destroy the ozone layer, which shields life on Earth from harmful ultraviolet radiation. The world responded with the **Montreal Protocol**, adopted in 1987, which phased out CFCs. Manufacturers switched largely to **R-134a**, a hydrofluorocarbon (HFC) that does not harm the ozone layer.

But HFCs turned out to be powerful greenhouse gases. According to the US Environmental Protection Agency, R-134a has a global warming potential (GWP) of about 1,430, meaning one kilogram traps roughly as much heat over a century as 1,430 kilograms of carbon dioxide. In 2016, countries agreed to the **Kigali Amendment** to the Montreal Protocol, committing to phase down HFCs.

Today, many household refrigerators, especially in Europe and Asia, use **isobutane (R-600a)**, a natural hydrocarbon with a GWP of about 3. Isobutane is flammable, so fridges that use it contain only a small charge of refrigerant, and their electrical parts are designed to avoid sparks near the refrigerant circuit. You can usually find the refrigerant type on the rating plate inside the fridge or on the back. It is one reason not to puncture the tubing when moving or scrapping an old fridge, and why old appliances should be disposed of through proper recycling channels that recover the refrigerant.

## Cousins of the fridge: air conditioners and heat pumps

Once you understand a refrigerator, you understand a whole family of machines. An **air conditioner** is a refrigerator whose "inside" is your room. Its evaporator sits in the indoor unit, where a fan blows room air across the cold coil; its compressor and condenser sit in the outdoor unit, which is why the air blowing out of it on a summer day is hot. The cold coil also pulls moisture out of the air, which drips away through the drain pipe you often see on the outside of buildings.

A **heat pump** used for heating runs the same cycle in reverse. A reversing valve swaps the roles of the two coils, so the outdoor coil becomes the evaporator, picking up heat even from chilly outdoor air, and the indoor coil becomes the condenser, releasing that heat into the home. Many modern "inverter air conditioners" can do both jobs.

### How efficient is a fridge?

Engineers describe the efficiency of these machines with a number called the **coefficient of performance (COP)**: the amount of heat moved divided by the electrical energy used to move it. Because a fridge is moving heat rather than creating it, its COP can be greater than 1. A compressor fridge typically moves somewhat more heat than the electricity it consumes, often between one and three times as much, depending on design and conditions.

COP falls as the temperature gap the machine must bridge grows. A fridge in a 25°C kitchen works less hard than the same fridge in a 38°C kitchen, and a freezer, which must hold -18°C, works harder than the fresh-food compartment. This is the physics behind two practical tips you will meet later: keep the fridge away from heat sources, and don't set it colder than you need.

It also explains why the efficiency of your fridge depends so much on its condenser. If dust or a tight cupboard stops the condenser from shedding heat, the refrigerant has to get hotter before it can condense, the compressor has to work harder to reach that higher pressure, and the COP drops.

## Inverter compressors and other modern features

### Inverter compressors

A traditional compressor is either fully on or fully off. When the inside warms past a threshold, it starts at full power; when the inside is cold enough, it stops. This on-off cycling wastes energy, especially at start-up, and causes the temperature inside to swing up and down.

An **inverter** (or variable-speed) compressor can run at different speeds. Most of the time it ticks along at a low speed, matching the cooling to the demand, and only speeds up when needed, for instance after you load a bag of warm groceries. Independent research and a US Department of Energy project on variable-capacity refrigerators point to energy savings on the order of 20 to 25 percent compared with conventional single-speed designs; some manufacturers advertise higher figures. Inverter fridges also tend to be quieter and keep a steadier temperature.

### Multiple evaporators and air flow

Cheaper fridges have a single evaporator and use a damper or vents to send some of the freezer's cold air into the fresh-food section. Some higher-end models have separate evaporators for the fridge and freezer, which helps keep humidity in the fresh-food area higher (good for vegetables) and prevents odours from travelling between compartments.

### Thermoelectric "fridges"

Small portable coolers and some mini-fridges use a **Peltier** (thermoelectric) module instead of a compressor: a solid-state device that moves heat from one face to the other when electric current flows through it. They are silent and simple, but far less efficient than compressor fridges, typically with a coefficient of performance well under 1, and they struggle to cool much below room temperature in a hot room. They are fine for keeping drinks cool in a car, not for storing meat safely in a tropical kitchen.

## Setting the right temperature

All the engineering above is only useful if the fridge is set correctly. Food safety agencies are clear on the target numbers:

- The **fridge compartment** should be at or below **4°C (40°F)**.
- The **freezer** should be at **-18°C (0°F)**.

These figures come from the US Food and Drug Administration, which recommends using an appliance thermometer to check, because the built-in dial rarely shows the actual temperature. Many people aim for around 3°C in the fridge to give a little margin, while avoiding temperatures so close to zero that lettuce and other delicate vegetables freeze.

Why 4°C? Because bacteria that cause food poisoning multiply fastest between 4°C and 60°C (40°F and 140°F), the range the US Department of Agriculture calls the **"Danger Zone"**. Refrigeration does not kill bacteria; it slows them down. Freezing stops them growing, but does not kill most of them either, which is why thawed food should be handled as carefully as fresh.

The USDA also advises not leaving perishable food out of the fridge for more than two hours, or more than one hour when the air temperature is above 32°C (90°F). In a hot climate, that one-hour rule applies for much of the year.

### How to check your fridge temperature

1. Put an appliance thermometer in a glass of water in the middle of the fridge.
2. Leave it for several hours or overnight, without opening the door much.
3. Read it. If it is above 4°C, turn the control colder and check again after 24 hours.
4. For the freezer, place the thermometer between frozen packages and check the same way.

## Where to put what: a map of your fridge

A refrigerator is not the same temperature everywhere. Cold air sinks, the area near the evaporator is coldest, and the door is the part most exposed to warm room air every time you open it.

- **Door shelves**: generally the warmest and most variable part. Good for condiments, sauces, juices and drinks, which are less sensitive. The USDA specifically advises keeping eggs in their carton in the coldest part of the fridge, **not in the door**, despite the egg trays many fridges have there. Milk also keeps better on an inside shelf than in the door.
- **Upper shelves**: fairly steady temperature. Good for leftovers, ready-to-eat foods, drinks and herbs.
- **Lower shelves**: usually the coldest part of the main compartment. Raw meat, poultry and fish belong here, ideally on a plate or in a container, so that their juices cannot drip onto other food.
- **Crisper drawers**: designed to keep humidity under control. Many have a slider. As appliance makers such as Whirlpool explain, the **high-humidity** setting (vent closed) suits leafy greens, herbs and vegetables that wilt; the **low-humidity** setting (vent open) suits fruits that give off ethylene gas, such as apples, pears, avocados and melons, because the gas can escape rather than speeding up ripening and spoilage around them. Keeping ethylene producers away from leafy greens helps both last longer.
- **Freezer**: keep it reasonably full (frozen items act as "cold batteries"), label and date what you put in, and use a first-in, first-out rule.

### The hot-food myth

Many people were taught never to put hot food in the fridge. The USDA's guidance is the opposite: hot food can go directly into the refrigerator, or be cooled quickly in an ice or cold-water bath first. The real risk is leaving food to cool slowly on the counter in the Danger Zone. The sensible precaution is to divide large amounts, like a big pot of soup or a tray of rice, into shallow containers so they cool quickly and evenly, and to leave a little space around them so cold air can circulate.

## Saving energy with your fridge

Because a refrigerator runs all the time, small habits add up over its lifetime. A modern, efficient full-size refrigerator often uses somewhere in the region of 350 to 650 kWh per year depending on size and design; the US Department of Energy cites one example of an ENERGY STAR model using about 364 kWh a year, against about 404 kWh for a less efficient comparable one. Older fridges, especially those with worn seals or dirty coils, can use much more. Here is how to keep yours at the efficient end:

1. **Give it room to breathe.** The condenser needs to shed heat. Leave the gap at the back and sides that the manual recommends, and do not put the fridge right next to an oven or in direct sunlight.
2. **Clean the condenser.** Dust and pet hair on the coils, or on the grille at the bottom, act like a blanket. Unplug the fridge and vacuum the coils once or twice a year.
3. **Check the door seal.** A popular test is to close the door on a sheet of paper or a banknote. If it slides out with almost no resistance, the gasket may not be sealing well at that spot. Try several places around the door. Cleaning the gasket with warm soapy water sometimes fixes it; otherwise it can be replaced.
4. **Don't set it colder than needed.** Every degree colder than necessary costs energy. Stick to about 3 to 4°C for the fridge and -18°C for the freezer.
5. **Keep it sensibly full, not crammed.** A reasonably full fridge holds its temperature better when you open the door, but blocking the air vents inside stops cold air circulating.
6. **Open the door less, and briefly.** Decide what you want before you open it.
7. **Let leftovers cool a little, then refrigerate promptly,** in shallow containers, rather than putting in a huge steaming pot.
8. **Defrost manual freezers** before the ice gets thicker than about half a centimetre or so; thick ice cuts efficiency.
9. **Level the fridge.** Many fridges are designed to tilt slightly backwards so the door swings shut on its own. Adjust the front feet if your door drifts open.

## When the power goes out

Power cuts are common in many places, especially during storms. The key rule is simple: **keep the doors closed**. According to food safety guidance from the US government, a closed refrigerator keeps food safe for about **4 hours**. A full, closed freezer holds its temperature for about **48 hours**, or about **24 hours** if it is half full.

After the power returns, check the temperature. Perishable food such as meat, fish, dairy and cooked leftovers that has been above 4°C for more than two hours should be thrown away. Frozen food that still has ice crystals or is at 4°C or below can generally be refrozen, though its quality may suffer. When in doubt, throw it out: the smell test is not reliable, because the bacteria that cause food poisoning often do not change how food looks or smells.

## Troubleshooting common problems

Most fridge problems have a handful of usual suspects. Before calling a technician, check these:

**The fridge is not cold enough, but the freezer is fine.** On many frost-free fridges, cold air flows from the freezer into the fridge compartment through a vent or damper. If that vent is blocked by food, or ice has built up because the defrost system has failed, the fridge side warms up. Also check the temperature setting and the door seal.

**Neither compartment is cold.** Is the fridge plugged in and the light on? Is the compressor running (you can usually hear it or feel it vibrating)? Dirty condenser coils, a failed condenser fan or a failed compressor are possible causes. If the compressor clicks on and off repeatedly without running, a starting relay may be faulty.

**Water on the floor.** Often a blocked defrost drain: the meltwater cannot reach the drain pan and overflows inside, then leaks out. Clearing the drain hole with warm water often solves it. A cracked drain pan or a leaking water line (for ice makers and water dispensers) are other causes.

**Ice building up in a frost-free freezer.** Usually a door that is not sealing properly, letting humid air in, or a problem with the defrost heater, sensor or timer.

**Strange noises.** Some sounds are normal: humming from the compressor, clicks from the thermostat, gurgling as refrigerant flows, cracking as plastic expands and contracts, and sizzling during defrost. Loud buzzing, grinding or rattling may mean a fan blade is hitting ice or a part has come loose.

**The fridge runs all the time.** Check the door seal, the coils and the room temperature. In a very hot room, a fridge naturally runs much more. A refrigerant leak is also possible, but it requires a qualified technician, because the sealed system has to be opened, repaired, evacuated and recharged.

Never try to repair the sealed refrigerant circuit yourself. Apart from needing specialist tools, releasing refrigerant is bad for the environment, and isobutane is flammable.

## Choosing a new refrigerator: what actually matters

If you are shopping for a fridge, the engineering above translates into a few practical questions:

- **Size**: buy for how you actually shop and cook. Someone who shops daily at a market needs far less space than a family that stocks up once a week, and capacity charts from retailers are only rough guides. A half-empty giant fridge wastes energy; an overstuffed small one cools poorly.
- **Configuration**: top-freezer models are usually the most energy-efficient and affordable; bottom-freezer models put fresh food at eye level; side-by-side and French-door models offer more features but often use more energy.
- **Frost-free or manual**: frost-free is far more convenient. Manual-defrost models can be slightly more efficient and cheaper, which is why many chest freezers still use them.
- **Inverter compressor**: worth paying for if you can, for lower running costs, quieter operation and steadier temperatures.
- **Energy label**: compare the stated annual energy use in kWh, not just the star rating, since labels differ between countries and are updated over time.
- **Climate class**: fridges are designed for certain ambient temperature ranges. In a hot country, choose a model rated for tropical conditions (often labelled "T"), especially if it will sit in a warm kitchen or garage.
- **Refrigerant**: models using R-600a are now common and climate-friendlier.

## The quiet machine, understood

Once you know what is happening inside, the everyday behaviour of a fridge starts to make sense. The warm sides are the condenser giving away heat. The hum is the compressor squeezing refrigerant. The gurgle is the fluid rushing through the capillary tube. The occasional drip is the defrost cycle. And the cold air that greets you is not cold that has been "made", but heat that has been carefully picked up and carried away.

Look after the few things that matter (a clean condenser, a tight door seal, the right temperature, sensible loading) and this humble box will keep your food safe and your bills modest for many years.
